q: Name Corsica's grape synonyms for Sangiovese, Grenache and Vermentino.
accept: nielluccio and malvoisie
nielluccio sangiovese malvoisie de corse vermentino
nielluccio is sangiovese and malvoisie de corse is vermentino
ans: Nielluccio = Sangiovese; Malvoisie de Corse = Vermentino; Grenache keeps its own name — and Sciacarello is none of the three: DNA identifies it as Tuscany's Mammolo
exp: The Sciacarello trap: it is not a synonym for anything French.

q: Trace Corsican viticulture from the 1960s to today: the planting boom, the crisis that followed, and where the island stands now.
accept: algerian repatriates planted the eastern plain then eu vine pull cut it back
boom on the plaine orientale bulk wine fraud then grubbing up and a return to native grapes
1960s planting surge collapse in the 1970s now quality wine from indigenous varieties
pieds noirs bulk vineyard peaked over thirty thousand hectares now under seven thousand
planted for bulk wine after 1962 then torn out with eu subsidies now hillside native varieties
ans: Repatriates from newly independent Algeria arrived from 1962 and planted the flat eastern Plaine Orientale with high-yielding varieties — Carignan, Cinsaut, Alicante and hybrids — for bulk wine to blend into mainland vin de table. Plantings roughly tripled, passing 30,000 hectares by the mid-1970s. It ended in fraud, chaptalisation scandals and violence, the 1975 siege at Aléria being the flashpoint, and then in EEC grubbing-up subsidies that tore out the plain. The vineyard fell by roughly three quarters, to somewhere near 6,000 to 7,000 hectares today. What replaced it was the opposite proposition: hillside sites, indigenous Niellucciu, Sciacarellu and Vermentinu, an AOP structure built around Patrimonio, Ajaccio, Muscat du Cap Corse and Vin de Corse's villages, and one of the highest shares of organic farming in France, helped by the dry maritime wind.
exp: This history is why the island's statistics mislead: IGP Île de Beauté still carries the volume, while the AOPs are small and recent. It also explains the shape of the modern industry — the quality vineyard was almost entirely rebuilt from the 1980s onward on sites the boom had ignored, so continuity of plant material and of vine age is thin compared with mainland regions of similar prestige.

q: Describe the Seyssel appellation: its still wine, its sparkling wine, and the grapes behind each.
accept: still wine is altesse and the mousseux is molette with ten percent altesse
altesse for the still molette plus altesse for the sparkling
100% altesse still and a molette based mousseux by traditional method
seyssel blanc altesse seyssel mousseux molette and altesse
ans: Seyssel straddles the Rhône on the Savoie–Ain border and was recognised in 1942, making it one of Savoie's oldest appellations. The still white is 100% Altesse — taut, hazelnut-and-white-pepper, more serious than its obscurity suggests. Seyssel Mousseux is the historic wine: a traditional-method sparkler built on Molette, a neutral local white, with a minimum of 10% Altesse for aroma and lift. Molette is grown almost nowhere else on earth, which is the whole point of the appellation.
exp: Seyssel Mousseux was Savoie's export wine — shipped to Paris and London long before Crémant de Savoie arrived in the mid-2010s and absorbed most of the region's sparkling ambition. Naming Molette is the marker of a candidate who has read past the textbook summary of the Alps.

q: A grower ages Savagnin under voile but bottles it in a 75 cl bottle as Côtes du Jura Savagnin rather than as Vin Jaune. What does that tell you, and what would the Vin Jaune rules have demanded?
accept: either aged less than six years and three months or declassified on purpose
the wine fell short of the vin jaune ageing term or was declassified by choice
vin jaune needs six years three months under voile and a clavelin so this is shorter or voluntarily declassified
same sous voile technique without meeting the vin jaune term and bottle rule
ans: Vin Jaune requires 100% Savagnin, aged in cask sans ouillage for a minimum of six years and three months with at least sixty months under the veil, and it must be sold in the 62 cl clavelin. So a sous-voile Savagnin in a standard bottle is one of two things: aged for less than the legal term, or aged long enough but declassified by choice. Both happen deliberately. Producers pull barrels at three or four years wanting the nutty voile signature without the full sotolon load, and many prefer the 75 cl format because a clavelin is awkward to sell by the glass and reads to guests as a curiosity rather than a wine. The technique is identical; only the legal endpoint differs.
exp: The clavelin is a legal statement, not a stylistic one — a candidate who reads it as 'oxidative Jura white' will be caught out. Château-Chalon adds the further layer that its commission can refuse an entire vintage, in which case the wine falls back to Côtes du Jura anyway.

q: You are opening a mature Château-Chalon for a table. Talk through service — temperature, glassware, timing — and what you would put beside it.
accept: around 14 to 16 celsius in a tulip glass opened early with aged comte
cellar temperature decanted an hour ahead and served with comte and morels
serve at 14-16c in a white wine glass air it ahead comte chicken with morels
cool room temperature aired in advance pairs with comte walnuts and curry
ans: Serve it cool but never cold, around 14 to 16 degrees: at white-wine temperature the aromatics shut down and only the acetaldehyde bite shows. Use a tulip or a generous white-wine glass, not a flute and not a small pour — the wine needs surface area and air. Open it well ahead, an hour or more, or decant; it has spent six years in an oxidative cask and cannot be bruised. That same stability means the open bottle holds for days, even weeks, which makes a 62 cl clavelin a viable by-the-glass proposition. On the plate: aged Comté above all, poulet aux morilles à la crème with vin jaune in the sauce, walnuts, and mild curry — sotolon's fenugreek note meets the dish halfway.
exp: Service is where Master candidates lose points on this wine: over-chilling and under-aerating are both fatal, and the standard closing question is why an open bottle survives. The answer is that oxidation has already done its work — there is little left for air to take.
